prompt: how do i work out the mean of four numbers
reply: Add them all up, then share the total equally between them 🧮. Say your marks are 3, 7, 8 and 6. They add to 24, and 24 ÷ 4 = 6, so the mean is 6. [STEPS]Add every number|Count how many|Divide total by count[/STEPS] Now try 5, 5, 2 and 8 📐. [CHIPS]Check my answer|Mean of my scores|What is median[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is the mode in maths
reply: Mode is the most common value — think mode equals most 🎯. In 4, 7, 4, 2, 4 the number 4 turns up three times, so 4 is the mode. A shoe shop cares about mode: it stocks the size the most feet need 👟. [QUIZ]In 2, 9, 9, 4 what is the mode?[/QUIZ] [CHIPS]9|2|4[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is the range of a set of numbers
reply: Range measures spread, not size 📏. [STEPS]Find the biggest|Find the smallest|Subtract smallest from biggest[/STEPS] In 12, 5, 9, 20 the range is 20 − 5 = 15. Two batters can average 30 each, but the steadier one has the smaller range 🏏. Your turn — the range of 6, 6, 14? [CHIPS]Range of my marks|Why spread matters|Steady vs streaky[/CHIPS]

prompt: why does a bar chart need a scale

prompt: what is the chance of rolling a 6 on a dice
reply: One in six 🎲. Six faces, one of them a 6, so roughly one roll in six lands a six. But on average is not a promise — you could roll thirty times and get eight sixes 🎯. Grab a dice, roll it thirty times, and see what your own count does.

reply: Both count the same thing, they just dress differently 📊. A bar chart uses height against a number scale. A pictogram repeats a symbol plus a key — one 🚌 might stand for 10 buses, so half a bus means 5. Pictograms look friendly but go awkward the moment you need 7. prompt: if i flip a coin 10 times will i get exactly 5 heads
reply: Usually not, and that is completely normal 🪙. Five is the single most likely result, but it shows up only about a quarter of the time — all the other splits share the rest. Flip 100 times and the share of heads creeps nearer to half, without ever owing you a tidy number 🎯. [CHIPS]Try 100 flips|Why not exactly half|What is fair[/CHIPS]

prompt: why do two dice make 7 more often than 12
reply: Count the routes, not the totals 🎲. Only 6 and 6 makes 12 — one route. But 7 has six routes: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1. Six routes beat one route, every single time 📊. [FACT]Two dice have 36 possible outcomes altogether[/FACT] [CHIPS]Ways to make 5|Tally my rolls|Roll fifty times[/CHIPS]

prompt: why do people use the median for salaries instead of the mean
reply: Because one enormous salary drags the mean along with it 💼. Picture nine people earning ₹3 lakh and one earning ₹100 lakh: the mean lands at ₹12.7 lakh, which describes nobody in that room. The median takes the middle of the lined-up list — ₹3 lakh — so the outlier cannot bully it. That is why serious reports quote median income 📊. [CHIPS]Find a median|When mean wins|What is an outlier[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is an outlier and should i just delete it
reply: An outlier sits far outside the pack, and deleting one is a decision, not a cleanup 🔍. Sometimes it is a typo — a person 1700 cm tall is a slipped decimal point. Sometimes it is the whole story: one faulty battery in 500 is exactly what a safety test is hunting for. Investigate first, and if you drop it, say so in your report 📋. [FACT]Removing an outlier shifts the mean far more than the median[/FACT] [CHIPS]Spot outliers in data|Mean vs median again|Real data example[/CHIPS]

prompt: the coin has landed tails five times so heads is due now right
reply: It feels overwhelmingly true, and it is wrong 🪙. The coin has no memory and no ledger — the next flip is still fifty-fifty, exactly like the first. What happens instead is dilution: as flips pile up, those five extra tails become a smaller slice of the total, so the share drifts toward half. Nothing ever evens the count out, and the mistake has a name — the gambler's fallacy 🎯. [CHIPS]Test it 200 times|Law of large numbers|Where else this tricks[/CHIPS]

prompt: what does a 30 percent chance of rain actually mean
reply: It describes many days, not your particular afternoon ☔. Roughly: out of 100 past days that looked like today, rain reached that spot on about 30 of them. So a dry afternoon at 30% is not a failed forecast — it is the other 70 showing up. Services differ a little in how they blend likelihood with how much of the area gets wet 🌦️. [QUIZ]A dry afternoon after a 30% forecast — was the forecast wrong?[/QUIZ] [CHIPS]No|Yes|Always wrong[/CHIPS]

prompt: is a sample of 100 people enough to know what a country thinks
reply: Size matters far less than fairness 🎯. A properly random sample of about 1,000 gives a margin of error near 3 points, and doubling it barely helps. But a biased sample of a million stays biased. In 1936 the Literary Digest collected over two million replies and still called the wrong winner — its address lists reached mostly car and telephone owners, and mostly the keen wrote back 📉. [CHIPS]Margin of error|Design a fair sample|Other poll failures[/CHIPS]

prompt: does correlation mean one thing caused the other
reply: No, and this is the trap that catches professionals too 🧠. Ice cream sales and drowning numbers rise together, yet neither causes the other — summer heat drives both. That hidden third factor is called a confounder. The only dependable way to claim cause is an experiment where you change one thing at random and hold the rest still 🔬. [FACT]Statisticians call that hidden shared cause a confounding variable[/FACT] [CHIPS]What is a confounder|Design an experiment|Famous false links[/CHIPS]

prompt: why can a pie chart be misleading
reply: A pie asks your eye to compare angles, which eyes are genuinely bad at — a 22% slice and a 25% slice are very hard to tell apart in a circle 🥧. Tilt it into 3D and the near slices swell for free. Worst of all, a pie insists the parts add to one whole, so any survey where people ticked several answers breaks it. A plain bar chart usually reads truer 📊. [CHIPS]When pies work|Bar chart instead|Test my eye[/CHIPS]

prompt: are dice rolls actually random or just too hard to predict
reply: A tumbling dice obeys ordinary mechanics, so in principle its landing is already settled 🎲. But it is chaotic: a hair's difference in spin or bounce flips the outcome, so prediction collapses in practice. So we model it as random, and the model works beautifully — which is also why a worn or weighted dice really can bias the result 🔍. Roll a dice sixty times and tally it — could sixty rolls ever prove it fair?

prompt: what does margin of error mean when they report a poll
reply: It is the width of the fuzz around the headline number 📊. 46% with a margin of error of 3 points means the true value probably sits between 43 and 49, usually at 95% confidence. So a poll showing 46 against 44 is too close to call, not a real lead. And it only covers random sampling — not people who lie or refuse to answer 🔍. prompt: if i shuffle a deck properly has that order ever happened before

Even if every human who ever lived shuffled once a second since the Big Bang, you would not scratch the surface ✨. prompt: our school survey got 40 replies out of 900 students is that a problem
reply: The count is small, but the bigger worry is who chose to reply 🎯. Forty out of 900 is under 5%, and the people who bother to answer are rarely a random slice — the strongly annoyed and the strongly keen arrive first. That is response bias, and no amount of careful maths repairs it afterwards. Better fix: pick 40 students at random and chase those 40 until they answer 📋. [CHIPS]What is response bias|Chase a random sample|Rewrite our survey[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i decide between mean median and mode for a report
reply: Ask what the number has to do for your reader 📐. Mean fits when values cluster and each one should pull its weight, like test scores. Median fits when a few extremes distort the picture — house prices, salaries, response times. Mode fits when the data is not numeric at all: most-chosen bus route, most-sold shoe size 📊. [QUIZ]House prices across a town — mean or median?[/QUIZ] [CHIPS]Median|Mean|Mode[/CHIPS]
